systemArchitecture.description: Syncfusion Cody is a next-generation AI-powered Integrated Development Environment (IDE) designed to enhance developer productivity. It combines AI with comprehensive development tools and deep integration with Syncfusion's component library. The architecture follows a multi-modal, context-aware design with pluggable configuration and extensible context providers.

components.name: Chat Mode
components.description: Natural language interaction with AI assistant. Users can ask coding questions, request code generation, and get explanations. Supports code selection via keyboard shortcuts (Cmd+L on Mac, Ctrl+L on Windows) to send selected code to chat.

components.name: Agent Mode
components.description: Autonomous AI assistant that works independently to explore code, plan updates, and complete complex tasks. Uses available tools to search, edit, create files, and run terminal commands. Requires user permission before executing tools.

components.name: Edit Mode
components.description: Targeted code modification with AI assistance. Users highlight code and specify updates. Changes appear inline for review. Supports accept/reject workflow per change or batch operations.

components.name: Autocomplete Mode
components.description: Real-time inline code suggestions as users type. Provides context-aware completions based on current code and project context. Requires 'autocomplete' role configuration in models section.

components.name: Configuration System
components.description: YAML-based configuration file (config.yaml) that manages all aspects of Cody behavior. Loaded from user settings with gear icon access point.

components.name: Model Management
components.description: Manages language models from various providers (OpenAI, Ollama, Mistral, etc.). Models can be assigned specific roles (chat, edit, autocomplete, apply, embed, rerank) and custom capabilities (tool_use, image_input).

components.name: Context Provider System
components.description: Modular context providers that deliver supplementary information to language models. Includes: file, code, codebase, docs, diff, http, folder, terminal, and other sources.

components.name: Rules Engine
components.description: Defines behavioral constraints and patterns for LLMs. Rules are combined into system message for Chat, Edit, and Agent requests. Supports glob-based file matching for context-specific rules.

components.name: Custom Prompts
components.description: User-defined prompts with name, description, and content. Can be invoked from the chat window. Enables task automation and workflow customization.

components.name: Documentation Indexing
components.description: Crawls and indexes documentation sites to provide context to language models. Supports web crawling with configurable depth, local-only crawling, and favicon configuration.

components.name: MCP Server Integration
components.description: Model Context Protocol server support for unified prompts, context, and tool use. Allows Cody to connect with any MCP-compliant server. Configured with command, args, environment variables, and connection timeout.

components.name: IDE Integration Layer
components.description: Bridges Cody with the underlying IDE. Provides code editing, file operations, terminal execution, and permission management for autonomous operations.

components.name: UI Builder (Syncfusion Integration)
components.description: AI-powered UI generation specifically integrated with Syncfusion components for rapid UI development.

systemArchitecture.organizationPattern: Modular, configuration-driven architecture with clear separation between features (Chat, Edit, Agent, Autocomplete) and core services (Models, Context, Rules, Configuration). Extensible through MCP servers and custom prompts.

serviceInteractions.description: Cody employs a hub-and-spoke architecture where the Configuration System acts as the central orchestrator. Models consume Context Provider outputs, and Rules/Prompts are applied during LLM invocation. Agent Mode coordinates multiple components for autonomous execution.

interactions.description: Features invoke configured models for LLM operations. Model selection depends on assigned roles.
Models receive context from multiple providers. Context is gathered before LLM invocation.
Rules are combined into system message for every Chat, Edit, and Agent request. Rules can be conditionally applied based on file globs.
Custom prompts can be invoked from the chat window for task automation.
Agent requests permission before using IDE tools for file search, editing, creation, and terminal execution.
Configuration file is the source of truth for all feature behavior, model selection, context providers, rules, and prompts.
Documentation context is indexed and made available through context providers.
MCP servers provide additional tools and context through the Model Context Protocol standard.
Edit mode works through the IDE: users select code in editor, Ed accepts/rejects diffs through IDE UI.
Autocomplete suggestions appear inline as users type in the IDE editor.

dataFlowArchitecture.flow: User Input → Feature Mode → Configuration Lookup → Model Selection → Context Gathering (multiple providers) → Rules Application → LLM Invocation → Response Generation → IDE Integration (for display/execution)

dataDesign.description: Configuration-driven data model using YAML schema. All runtime behavior is declaratively specified in config.yaml. Data structures are hierarchical and composable, following a clear separation between configuration metadata, runtime context, and user prompts.

designPatterns.description: Cody demonstrates several well-established design patterns that make it extensible, maintainable, and configuration-driven.

patterns.name: Configuration-Driven Architecture
patterns.description: All behavior is declaratively specified in config.yaml rather than hardcoded. This enables flexibility and user customization without code changes.

advantages: No deployment required for configuration changes

patterns.name: Multi-Modal Feature Design
patterns.description: Cody offers multiple interaction modes (Chat, Edit, Agent, Autocomplete) that are independently selectable and configurable. Each mode serves different user workflows.
patterns.advantage: Users can choose mode appropriate to their task, reducing friction

patterns.name: Plugin Architecture (Context Providers)
patterns.description: Context is provided by pluggable providers (file, code, codebase, docs, diff, http, folder, terminal, problems, helpbot). New providers can be added by implementing the provider interface.
patterns.extensibility: Each provider accepts optional 'params' for customization

patterns.name: Role-Based Capability Dispatch
patterns.description: Models are assigned roles (chat, autocomplete, edit, apply, embed, rerank). Features select models based on required role. Decouples feature implementation from model selection.

patterns.name: System Message Composition
patterns.description: Rules are conditionally applied based on file context and combined into the system message for LLM invocation. Supports glob-based rule filtering.

implementation.simpleRules: Plain text applied to all requests
implementation.namedRules: Objects with name, rule, and optional globs
implementation.conditionalApplication: Rules applied only when file matches glob patterns

patterns.name: Agentic Loop Pattern
patterns.description: Agent mode implements a well-defined workflow: Understand → Explore → Plan → Execute → Verify → Complete. Each step is explicit and the agent seeks permission before tool execution.
patterns.permissionModel: Explicit user approval required before tool invocation

patterns.name: Keyboard Shortcut Accessibility Pattern
patterns.description: Common operations are accessible via keyboard shortcuts, enabling quick access for power users.
patterns.evidence: Chat.md lines 17; Edit.md lines 19-20; Autocomplete.md lines 33-39

patterns.name: Prompt Template Pattern
patterns.description: Custom prompts can be defined as templates with name, description, and content. These can be invoked from the chat window for task automation.
patterns.advantage: Enables workflow automation and task standardization

patterns.name: Protocol Bridge Pattern (MCP Integration)
patterns.description: MCP servers are bridged via process execution. Cody launches external processes that implement the MCP protocol, following Anthropic's standard.

patterns.name: Web Crawling & Indexing Pattern
patterns.description: Documentation sites are crawled with configurable depth and indexed to provide contextual knowledge to LLMs.

patterns.name: Accept/Reject Review Pattern
patterns.description: Both Edit mode and Agent mode present changes for user approval before applying. Supports individual and batch review.

antiPatterns.description: Potential architectural concerns and suboptimal design decisions that could limit scalability, maintainability, or user experience.

issues.description: All behavior (models, context, rules, prompts, docs, MCP servers) is defined in a single config.yaml file. This can become unwieldy as configuration grows.
issues.evidence: Configure-the-Cody.md lines 84-115; multiple configuration examples show single monolithic YAML
issues.impact: Maintainability at scale; UX for configuration management
issues.recommendation: Support configuration composition/inheritance or split configuration by domain (models.yaml, contexts.yaml, rules.yaml, etc.)

issues.description: Documentation does not specify error handling, fallback behavior, or recovery mechanisms for various failure scenarios.
issues.evidence: No error handling documentation across any reference files
issues.impact: Unpredictable behavior in production; poor user experience during failures
issues.recommendation: Define and document error handling strategy: timeout handling, circuit breakers, fallback models, graceful degradation

issues.description: config.yaml examples show API keys directly in the configuration file (Configure-the-Cody.md line 91: 'apiKey: original key'). This is a security anti-pattern.
issues.recommendation: Mandate environment variable injection for credentials; document best practices for credential management (environment variables, credential managers)

issues.description: External services (LLM providers, MCP servers) are referenced without version pinning or compatibility guarantees.
issues.evidence: models.md and mcpServers.md do not mention version constraints; docs.md does not specify crawler version
issues.impact: Unpredictable behavior after dependency updates; difficult debugging
issues.recommendation: Support version pinning for models, MCP servers, and documentation crawler

issues.description: Multiple context providers are aggregated but no documented strategy for context token management or priority.
issues.evidence: context.md lines 45-59 shows all providers active without token management
issues.impact: Unpredictable LLM behavior at scale; potential cost overruns with large contexts
issues.recommendation: Document context prioritization, add token counting, support context truncation strategies

issues.description: Some features lack detailed documentation on capabilities, limitations, and best practices.
issues.evidence: Features documented but without detailed examples or troubleshooting guides
issues.recommendation: Add feature interaction examples, troubleshooting guides, and FAQ

issues.description: Only Windows and macOS are documented. Linux support is not mentioned.
issues.evidence: get-started/ contains only Windows.md and Mac.md; no Linux.md
issues.recommendation: Document Linux installation and support; clarify Docker/container deployment

issues.description: Agent mode requires permission for each tool use but does not support fine-grained permissions (e.g., allow read-only, deny network access).
concerns: Unable to limit agent capabilities per tool
issues.evidence: Agent.md lines 49-56 show binary permission prompts
issues.impact: Security risk for unattended agent use; operational constraints
issues.recommendation: Support fine-grained permissions per tool type or resource

issues.description: Configuration and context are user-global with no isolation for multi-user environments.
issues.evidence: config.yaml is assumed to be per-user but no multi-tenant support mentioned
issues.impact: Unsuitable for team environments; security risk
issues.recommendation: Support workspace/project-level configuration with user isolation

issues.description: No documented strategy for validating config.yaml or detecting misconfiguration.
concerns: Unavailable MCP servers not detected until runtime
Circular prompt references or invalid globs not validated
issues.evidence: No validation documentation across reference files
issues.impact: Runtime errors from misconfiguration; poor debugging experience
issues.recommendation: Document configuration validation, add schema validation, provide clear error messages

scalabilityRisks.description: Architectural limitations and design decisions that could impede scalability, performance, or operational resilience.

risks.description: As configuration complexity grows (more context providers, rules, docs, MCP servers) and codebase size increases, total context tokens could exceed LLM limits, causing failures or expensive truncation.
risks.consequence: LLM failures, degraded performance, unpredictable behavior
risks.evidence: No token management or context prioritization in documentation
risks.mitigationStrategy: Implement context budgeting, prioritization, and selective provider activation

risks.description: Single config.yaml grows without bound as users add more models, context providers, rules, and custom prompts. No hierarchical organization.
risks.consequence: Configuration becomes unwieldy, difficult to maintain, prone to merge conflicts
risks.evidence: All configuration in single file as shown in Configure-the-Cody.md
risks.mitigationStrategy: Support configuration composition, namespacing, or hierarchical configuration structure

risks.description: Web crawling for documentation sites with large maxDepth values or many docs could cause startup delays or performance issues.
risks.consequence: Slow startup, indexing bottlenecks, resource exhaustion
risks.evidence: docs.md lines 35-37 show configurable maxDepth with default 4; no performance guidance
risks.mitigationStrategy: Add crawling performance metrics, async indexing, caching strategy

risks.description: MCP servers are spawned as external processes. Multiple servers without proper resource management could exhaust system resources.
risks.consequence: Resource exhaustion, system instability, zombie processes
risks.evidence: mcpServers.md shows process-based launch mechanism; no resource management documented
risks.mitigationStrategy: Implement process pooling, resource limits, graceful shutdown, and leak detection

risks.description: If one context provider fails (e.g., HTTP context server down, filesystem error), it could block all LLM invocations.
risks.evidence: context.md lines 45-59 show multiple providers; no failure handling documented
risks.mitigationStrategy: Implement provider circuit breakers, timeouts, and graceful degradation

risks.description: API keys and credentials in config.yaml could be logged or exposed in error messages, telemetry, or crash dumps.
risks.evidence: Configure-the-Cody.md line 91 shows credentials in config examples
risks.mitigationStrategy: Implement credential masking in logs, use environment variables only, disable credential logging

risks.description: Different models assigned to different roles (chat, edit, autocomplete) could produce inconsistent responses, confusing users.
triggers: Mixing different model families (GPT, Claude, Mistral)
Different model versions for different roles
risks.evidence: models.md allows arbitrary model combinations without guidance on consistency
risks.mitigationStrategy: Provide model combo presets, document consistency implications, add model capability detection

risks.description: Agent mode loops through Understand → Explore → Plan → Execute → Verify until task complete. No documented timeout or max iteration limits could cause infinite loops.
risks.evidence: Agent.md lines 28-46 describe workflow but no termination conditions
risks.mitigationStrategy: Implement max iterations, timeout, and explicit task completion criteria

risks.description: As projects grow, number of context-specific rules could explode, making rule management unmaintainable.
triggers: Many file types with different rules
risks.evidence: rules.md shows per-file glob matching but no rule inheritance or composition
risks.mitigationStrategy: Support rule templates, inheritance, and composition patterns

risks.description: config.yaml exists per user/machine. No centralized management, versioning, or synchronization.
risks.consequence: Inconsistent behavior across team, difficult debugging, compliance issues
risks.evidence: config.yaml is local per user; no team/organization-level configuration management
risks.mitigationStrategy: Support centralized configuration server, environment promotion, audit trails
